title: Why keep it?
hookLine: reasons offered include holiness, discipline and identity; some laws are kept simply as commands

cards: Someone at work sees your friend turn down the shrimp at a party and asks, a little too loudly: but why? It's not like pork is dangerous anymore. Is it a health thing?
Your friend has maybe ten seconds to answer. What do they say? People who keep kosher hear it often.
And here's the honest thing: Jewish tradition has offered many answers over the centuries, and one rabbi said the best answer might be no reason at all.

teach.b: The rabbis sorted the Torah's laws into kinds. Mishpatim, judgments, are laws any society would reach on its own, like don't murder, don't steal. Chukim are different.
A chok is a statute, a decree, from a root meaning to engrave or inscribe: a law the Torah gives without a reason, one reason alone wouldn't produce.

teach.h: THIS IS THE STATUTE OF THE LAW.
teach.b: The classic example is the red heifer, introduced with the words "This is the statute of the law." The Talmud's own list of chukim includes eating pork. So why keep them?
Jewish thinkers have offered several answers, side by side.
Holiness: near the end of the chapter on food, the Torah says, "ye shall therefore be holy, for I am holy."
Kadosh, holy, is often explained as set apart, and a daily set-apart practice makes ordinary life point somewhere. Discipline: Maimonides taught that the food laws train a person to rein in appetite.
Identity: across the centuries, a shared table has helped keep a scattered people recognizable to one another. Eat in a kosher home in Buenos Aires or Paris or Tel Aviv, and you know the rules.
And then there's the Sifra, an early midrash on Leviticus. A rabbi named Elazar ben Azariah said: don't say, I can't stand pork.
Say, I would like to, but what can I do?
My Father in heaven has decreed. The point isn't disgust. It's choosing to keep a commandment, even without a reason.
Some who keep it describe that less as obedience than as loyalty and love: like doing something because someone you love asked.

how: Jews who keep kosher give many reasons: holiness, discipline, identity, or simply that it's a commandment. Many say that keeping a law without a stated reason is itself an act of devotion.

o: a rule that exists to protect your health
a law kept even though no reason is given
a law any fair society would reach by itself

games.q: what's inside the reasons — tap the pairs.

s: Jewish tradition gives one official reason for keeping kosher
it offers several side by side: holiness, discipline, identity, love of the commandment.
a chok is a law the Torah gives without a stated reason
the red heifer is the classic example.
the midrash says the ideal is to find pork disgusting
it says: I would like to, but my Father in heaven has decreed.

games.q: a coworker asks why you won't eat the shrimp. following Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah, what do you say?
o: it's disgusting and bad for you.
I'd like to, but it's a commandment I keep.
games.why: he taught: don't say I can't stand it. say I would like to, but my Father in heaven has decreed. the point is choosing to keep it.

practice: Pick one small food rule to keep for a day: no sugar in the coffee, no eating standing up, saying thanks before each meal. Nothing extreme, and nothing unsafe for your health.
Notice that you don't have to explain it to anyone, then picture the moment you'll want to break it, and what you'll remember then.

wordCard.voice: Chok. A statute: a commandment given without a stated reason, and kept anyway, out of holiness, discipline, identity or love.
